transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for calling S-Net technical support, my name is Priya. Could I start with the account number on the line so I can bring up the record?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hi Priya. Yes, it's 771-460-238. The account should be under Dana Whitfield.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Got it, thank you Dana. I have the account open in front of me now. I'm showing a 500 meg fibre business line at the service address. What's going on today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So this is driving me a little bit crazy. My wired desktop, the one I actually work on, keeps losing its network connection. It'll be fine for twenty minutes and then just drop, and Windows shows that little globe icon with no internet. It comes back by itself after a minute or so, but it's happened maybe fifteen times since Monday.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That sounds genuinely disruptive, Dana, and I'm sorry you've been fighting with it since Monday. Fifteen drops in a few days on a machine you work on is not something you should have to work around. I'll stay with you on this until we understand what's actually causing it.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you. I've been putting it off because I assumed it'd take all afternoon to sort out.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let's see if we can do better than that. Before I touch anything, let me play back what you've told me so I know I've got it right. Your wired desktop loses connectivity roughly every twenty minutes, Windows reports no internet, and it recovers on its own after about a minute without you doing anything. Is that accurate?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's exactly it. Spot on.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And the important follow-up: when the desktop drops, does anything else in the house drop at the same time? Phone, laptop, TV?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, and that's the weird part. My laptop is sitting right next to it on Wi-Fi and it never drops. My partner works upstairs on Wi-Fi too and she's had no complaints at all.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That is a really useful answer, because it rules out a great deal in one go. If the fibre line or the router itself were dropping, everything would go down together. The fact that it's one wired machine while Wi-Fi stays up points us at the wired path specifically.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, that makes sense. I hadn't thought of it that way.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let's map that path out. Is the desktop plugged directly into the S-Net router, or is there something in between?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: There's something in between. The router's downstairs in the hall and my office is at the back of the house, so I'm using a pair of powerline adapters through the mains. One plugs in by the router, the other by my desk.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Powerline adapters. That's a very strong candidate, and I'll explain why in a moment. What operating system is the desktop running?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Windows 11.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you. And roughly how old is the powerline pair, and do you know the brand?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: They're TP-Link, and honestly they're old. I'd guess five or six years? They came with me from the last flat.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's helpful. Powerline adapters send data over your household electrical wiring, and they are quite sensitive to what else is plugged into the same circuit. A fridge compressor, a laser printer, even a phone charger on a shared socket can inject noise that knocks the link down briefly and then lets it recover. That recovery pattern is exactly what you're describing.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Huh. There's a small chest freezer in the utility room, and I think that's on the same side of the house.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Then that's worth keeping in mind. But I don't want to jump to the answer before we've tested it, because there are two or three other things that produce the same symptom and I'd rather be right than fast. Can I take you through some checks?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, absolutely. What do you need?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: First one is easy. Are both powerline adapters plugged directly into wall sockets, or is either one in an extension lead or a surge protector?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The one by my desk is in a surge-protected extension strip. The one downstairs is straight in the wall.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Right. That's a real finding. Surge protectors are specifically designed to filter out electrical noise, and powerline adapters communicate using what looks like electrical noise. Putting one behind a surge protector can cut its throughput substantially or make the link unstable. Manufacturers all say to plug them straight into the wall.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Nobody told me that. It's been like that for years.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It's a genuinely common setup and it's not your fault, the instructions bury it. Could you move that adapter out of the strip and into a wall socket directly for me?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Give me a second, I'll crawl under the desk. Okay... unplugged from the strip... and it's now in the wall socket by the skirting board. The light on it just went orange, now it's green.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Green is what we want. Let's leave it there. Now, while we see whether that holds, I want to check the other end of the path. Can you open the Network settings on the desktop for me?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Sure. I've got the network page up.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Under the Ethernet connection there should be a properties or details view showing the link speed. Could you tell me what it says?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Let me find it... it says one hundred megabits per second.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: There we go. That's the second finding, and it's a significant one. Your line is 500 meg, and your adapter is negotiating at 100. So even when it's not dropping, that connection is capped at a fifth of what you're paying for.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Wait, seriously? I've been running at a hundred this whole time?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: On that wired path, yes. Now, older powerline adapters do have 100 meg ports, so this may simply be the hardware. But a damaged or low-grade ethernet cable will also force a connection down to 100, so we should check that before we blame the adapter.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: How would I tell the difference?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Look at the cable running from the adapter to the desktop. Printed along the jacket there should be a category marking. Cat5, Cat5e, Cat6, something like that.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hang on, let me get my glasses. It's very small print... I can see CAT5. Just CAT5, no letter after it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's your answer on the cable. Plain Cat5, without the e, is only rated for 100 megabits. It physically cannot carry gigabit. So even with a brand new adapter you'd still be capped.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So I need a new cable.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You need a Cat5e or Cat6 cable, yes, and they're inexpensive. Do you happen to have a spare anywhere? Sometimes there's one in the box the router came in.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Actually, there might be. The S-Net box is still in the cupboard because I never throw anything away. Let me look.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Take your time, Dana.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, found the box. There's a yellow cable still in its bag, never opened. It says CAT6 on the wrapper.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's ideal. That cable will have come with your router and it's rated well beyond what you need. Could you swap it in for the Cat5 one between the adapter and the desktop?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Doing it now. Old one out... new one in, I heard it click at both ends. The little lights on the network port are flashing.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good. Give Windows a few seconds to renegotiate, then check that link speed reading again for me.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Refreshing... oh. It says one gigabit per second now.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Excellent. So that's the cap removed. To be clear about what we've done so far: we've taken the adapter out of the surge protector, which should help stability, and we've replaced a cable that was limiting your speed. Those are two separate problems that happened to be sitting on top of each other.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's good to know. But is that going to stop the dropping? That's the bit that's actually ruining my day.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It may well, and it may not, so let's not assume. There's a third thing I want to rule out, and it's a setting rather than hardware. Windows has a power saving feature that is allowed to switch off a network adapter when it thinks the machine is idle. When it does that, you get exactly what you're seeing: a drop out of nowhere that heals itself a minute later.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That sounds very much like it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It's a common one. What version of Windows is this again?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Windows 11. I did say that at the start.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You did, apologies. Windows 11. On that version, open Device Manager, expand Network adapters, and find the ethernet one, then open its properties.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay... Device Manager is open. Network adapters... there's a Realtek one and a couple of others. I'll open the Realtek.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That'll be it. There should be a Power Management tab along the top.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Got it. And there's a tick box that says allow the computer to turn off this device to save power. It's ticked.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's the one. Please untick it and click OK.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Done. Hang on, how long is this going to take overall? I've got a call at half past that I really can't be late for.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: We'll get through it. Let's carry on and see where we end up.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Alright.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: There's a related setting worth doing while we're here. Back on the Advanced tab of that same adapter, look for an entry called Energy Efficient Ethernet, or sometimes Green Ethernet.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Scrolling... yes, Energy Efficient Ethernet. It's set to Enabled.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Set that to Disabled for me. On a desktop that's on all day it saves a negligible amount of power, and it's known to cause link instability on certain Realtek chipsets.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Changed to Disabled. Clicked OK.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Dana, I'm going to put you on a brief hold while I look at the line diagnostics from our side. You'll hear music but I'm still working on this, and I'll come straight back.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No problem.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thanks very much for holding. I've pulled the last seven days of line statistics and I want to share what I'm seeing, because it's genuinely useful. Your fibre line shows no errors at all, no resyncs, no signal degradation. From the street to your router is completely clean.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So it really is all inside the house.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Everything points that way. Which is good news, because the things inside the house are things we can actually change. What I'd like to do now is watch the connection under load rather than wait around hoping it drops.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: How would we do that?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I'll have you run a continuous connectivity test from the desktop. It sends a small packet every second to our server and reports anything that fails to come back. If the link is still unstable, that will catch it within a few minutes instead of us waiting twenty.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, tell me what to type.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Open the Start menu, type cmd, and press enter to get a command prompt. Then type ping, space, minus t, space, and then eight dot eight dot eight dot eight, and press enter.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Command prompt is open... typed it in... and it's scrolling. Lots of lines saying reply from, with times around nine and ten milliseconds.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Nine to ten milliseconds is a healthy, stable latency. Let that run and tell me immediately if you see anything that says request timed out or destination host unreachable.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Will do. It's just scrolling steadily so far.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good. While that's running, let's deal with the freezer question you raised earlier, because I don't want to lose it. Do you know whether the socket your desk adapter is now in shares a circuit with the utility room?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I genuinely don't. The consumer unit is labelled but it's fairly vague. It just says downstairs sockets.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's typical, and it's fine. Rather than trying to trace it, here's a practical test you can do yourself later. Next time it drops, note whether the freezer has just kicked in. Compressors cycle every few hours, so if you see a pattern you'll have your answer without touching the wiring.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's a good idea. I can do that.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And if it does turn out to be the freezer, the fix isn't dramatic. Either move the adapter to a socket on a different circuit, or run a long ethernet cable along the skirting and take the powerline out of the equation entirely.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The cable would be more reliable, I'm guessing?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Considerably, yes. Powerline is a compromise for when running cable isn't practical. It's a reasonable compromise, but a physical cable removes an entire category of problems at once. It's worth thinking about if the drops come back.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Noted. The ping thing is still going, by the way. Still all replies, no timeouts.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's encouraging. How long has it been running now?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Maybe four minutes? I can see it's up to about two hundred and forty lines.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Two hundred and forty consecutive replies with no loss is a meaningfully good sign, given you were dropping every twenty minutes. Let's give it a bit more. Remind me, what brand were those powerline adapters?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: TP-Link. That's twice now I've told you that one.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You're quite right, I should have written it down. TP-Link, thank you, and I won't ask you again. The reason I wanted it is that TP-Link publish a utility that shows the actual link rate between the two adapters, which would tell us how much headroom you have on the mains.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Should I install that?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Not while we're on the call, but it's worth having later. I'll note the name on your account so you have it: it's the tpPLC utility on their support site.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Great, thank you.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Now, there's one more thing I'd like to do, and it does mean a short interruption. The network adapter changes we made will apply properly after a restart. Windows usually applies them live, but a restart makes certain, and I'd rather be certain than have you discover it tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay. How long will the restart take? I've got that call coming up.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It'll come back when it comes back. Go ahead and restart it and we'll pick up on the other side.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Right. Restarting now.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I'll stay on the line.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's going down... black screen... and it's coming back. Windows is loading. Okay, I'm at the desktop, and the network icon looks normal, no globe.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good. Let's confirm it properly rather than trust the icon. Could you reopen the ethernet properties and check the link speed once more?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Opening it... one gigabit per second. Still there.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And could you start that ping test again? Same command as before.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Running... replies coming back, nine milliseconds, ten milliseconds. Looks the same as before.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Dana, I'm going to put you on hold once more, just briefly, while I write all of this up on your account. Is that alright?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's fine.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for waiting. I've documented everything on the account: the surge protector, the Cat5 cable we replaced, both adapter power settings, and the note about the freezer circuit. If you ever do have to call back, whoever picks it up will see exactly what we changed rather than starting from scratch.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's genuinely helpful, thank you. The last time I called something in, I had to explain the whole thing twice.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Then I'm glad this one was different. Let's do a final check together. Could you open a browser and load a couple of sites, and tell me how they feel?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Loading... my email client came up straight away. A news site loaded instantly. It does feel faster, actually, noticeably.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That'll be the cable. You've gone from a hundred megabits to a gigabit on that machine, so everything that touches the network should feel quicker.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: And the ping is still running clean. No timeouts at all.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I want to be straight with you rather than overpromise. Ten minutes of clean pings doesn't prove it on its own, given your drops were roughly twenty minutes apart. What I can say with confidence is that we found and removed three separate things that each cause this exact symptom: the surge protector filtering the adapter, a cable that couldn't carry full speed, and a power setting allowed to switch your adapter off.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's fair. So what do I do if it happens again?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Two things. Note the time it drops and check whether the freezer has just kicked in, as we discussed. And if it's still dropping after a couple of days, call us back and quote this ticket, and the next step is running a physical cable to that room rather than going through the mains at all.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's clear. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Dana, before I let you go, I want to check the thing you actually came to us for. Based on what you're seeing on the screen right now, is the issue you called about resolved?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, I'd say so. It's up, it's faster than it's ever been, and it hasn't dropped once while we've been talking. And I know what to watch for now, which I didn't before.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's exactly what I was hoping to hear. And thank you for doing all the hands-on parts, the cable swap and crawling under the desk. That's what let us solve it properly today instead of booking an engineer visit.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Well, I appreciate you actually explaining things. I've learned more about my own network in twenty minutes than in five years.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's a lovely thing to hear. Is there anything else at all I can help you with on the account today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, I'm all set. You've been brilliant.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you very much, Dana. We do value your feedback, so please stay on the line for a brief one-question survey about my service today. Thank you for choosing S-Net, and I hope the rest of your day goes smoothly.
